To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

genetic correlations of litter sizes between adjacent parities are high, whereas genetic correlations are low between nonadjacent litter sizes; genetic correlations between growth traits and litter size are close to zero; and genetic correlations between litter size and backfat are low and negative.
genetic correlations between litter sizes for different parities are high, and genetic correlations of litter sizes between parities and production traits are low.

the heritability for litter size increases with the parity order and that genetic correlations between litter size in adjacent parities are high but low between nonadjacent ones, whereas the genetic correlations of litter sizes between growth and backfat are close to zero.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the estimation of genetic parameters for multiple parities of litter size and production traits in pigs.
the genetic correlation between production and reproduction traits.
the development of a Bayesian method for the estimation of variance component for litter size in pigs, which can be used to estimate the genetic parameters for multiple traits.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
genetic correlations among parities of litter size are moderate, and genetic correlations between production and litter size traits are low.
selection for litter size in pigs is not expected to have a significant effect on the production traits.
genetic correlations between parities are not high enough to allow the use of information from one parity for selection on litter size of the other parities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetic correlation between litter size in different parities is very low, which suggests that selection for litter size should not be based on the same trait in different parities.
genetic improvement of litter size is possible, but it will not result in correlated response in growth and backfat.

the genetic parameters for NBA in the first parity were very low, but increased with the parity number, and the genetic correlations between NBA in different parities were very high between adjacent parities, but much lower between non-adjacent parities, and the genetic correlation between NBA and growth and backfat were close to zero.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Bayesian approach is very effective in the analysis of complex models, such as the one presented in this paper, where there is a large number of parameters to estimate.
the genetic correlation between litter size in adjacent parities is high enough to justify the use of a multiple-trait model to estimate genetic parameters for litter size.
genetic correlations between litter size in different parities and between litter size and production traits should be considered when implementing selection strategies in pigs.
